Your dwarf character has an assortment of inborn abilities, part and parcel of dwarven nature.

Ability Score Increase. Your Constitution score increases by 2.

Age. Dwarves mature at the same rate as humans, but they're considered young until they reach the age of 50. On average, they live about 350 years.

Alignment. Most dwarves are lawful, believing firmly in the benefits of a well-ordered society. They tend toward good as well, with a strong sense of fair play and a belief that everyone deserves to share in the benefits of a just order.

Size. Dwarves stand between 4 and 5 feet tall and average about 150 pounds. Your size is Medium.

Speed. Your base walking speed is 25 feet. Your speed is not reduced by wearing heavy armor.

Darkvision. Accustomed to life underground, you have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You can't discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.

Dwarven Resilience. You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Dwarven Combat Training. You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.

Tool Proficiency. You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.

Stonecunning. Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.

Languages. You can speak, read, and write Common and Dwarvish. Dwarvish is full of hard consonants and guttural sounds, and those characteristics spill over into whatever other language a dwarf might speak.

Hill Dwarf

As a hill dwarf, you have keen senses, deep intuition, and remarkable resilience.

Ability Score Increase. Your Wisdom score increases by 1.

Dwarven Toughness. Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Foundry Note

Dwarven Toughness should be configured by adding 1 to the "Per Level" bonus in HP configuration on your character sheet (accessible using the cog next to your character's hit points).

You are a member of an artisan's guild, skilled in a particular field and closely associated with other artisans. You are a well-established part of the mercantile world, freed by talent and wealth from the constraints of a feudal social order. You learned your skills as an apprentice to a master artisan, under the sponsorship of your guild, until you became a master in your own right.

  • Skill Proficiencies: @skill[Insight], @skill[Persuasion]

  • Tool Proficiencies: One type of artisan's tools

  • Languages: One of your choice

  • Equipment: A set of artisan's tools (one of your choice), a letter of introduction from your guild, a set of @item[traveler's clothes|phb], and a belt @item[pouch|phb] containing 15 gp

Feature: Guild Membership[–]

As an established and respected member of a guild, you can rely on certain benefits that membership provides. Your fellow guild members will provide you with lodging and food if necessary, and pay for your funeral if needed. In some cities and towns, a guildhall offers a central place to meet other members of your profession, which can be a good place to meet potential patrons, allies, or hirelings.

Guilds often wield tremendous political power. If you are accused of a crime, your guild will support you if a good case can be made for your innocence or the crime is justifiable. You can also gain access to powerful political figures through the guild, if you are a member in good standing. Such connections might require the donation of money or magic items to the guild's coffers.

You must pay dues of 5 gp per month to the guild. If you miss payments, you must make up back dues to remain in the guild's good graces.

Specialty[–]

Guilds are generally found in cities large enough to support several artisans practicing the same trade. However, your guild might instead be a loose network of artisans who each work in a different village within a larger realm. Work with your DM to determine the nature of your guild. You can select your guild business from the Guild Business table or roll randomly.

Suggested Characteristics[–]

Guild artisans are among the most ordinary people in the world—until they set down their tools and take up an adventuring career. They understand the value of hard work and the importance of community, but they're vulnerable to sins of greed and covetousness.

[[/r d8]]Personality Trait
1I believe that anything worth doing is worth doing right. I can't help it—I'm a perfectionist.
2I'm a snob who looks down on those who can't appreciate fine art.
3I always want to know how things work and what makes people tick.
4I'm full of witty aphorisms and have a proverb for every occasion.
5I'm rude to people who lack my commitment to hard work and fair play.
6I like to talk at length about my profession.
7I don't part with my money easily and will haggle tirelessly to get the best deal possible.
8I'm well known for my work, and I want to make sure everyone appreciates it. I'm always taken aback when people haven't heard of me.
[[/r d6]]Ideal
1Community. It is the duty of all civilized people to strengthen the bonds of community and the security of civilization. (Lawful)
2Generosity. My talents were given to me so that I could use them to benefit the world. (Good)
3Freedom. Everyone should be free to pursue his or her own livelihood. (Chaotic)
4Greed. I'm only in it for the money. (Evil)
5People. I'm committed to the people I care about, not to ideals. (Neutral)
6Aspiration. I work hard to be the best there is at my craft. (Any)
[[/r d6]]Bond
1The workshop where I learned my trade is the most important place in the world to me.
2I created a great work for someone, and then found them unworthy to receive it. I'm still looking for someone worthy.
3I owe my guild a great debt for forging me into the person I am today.
4I pursue wealth to secure someone's love.
5One day I will return to my guild and prove that I am the greatest artisan of them all.
6I will get revenge on the evil forces that destroyed my place of business and ruined my livelihood.
[[/r d6]]Flaw
1I'll do anything to get my hands on something rare or priceless.
2I'm quick to assume that someone is trying to cheat me.
3No one must ever learn that I once stole money from guild coffers.
4I'm never satisfied with what I have—I always want more.
5I would kill to acquire a noble title.
6I'm horribly jealous of anyone who can outshine my handiwork. Everywhere I go, I'm surrounded by rivals.

The Icon of Ravenloft is a 12-inch tall statuette made of the purest silver, weighing 10 pounds. It depicts a cleric kneeling in supplication.

The icon was given to Strahd by the archpriest Ciril Romulich, an old family friend, to consecrate the castle and its chapel.

Augury.

One notable remnant from Waluigi’s destroyed airship is the Warped Gamma Propeller, a massive, twisted propeller blade that once powered the vessel’s erratic flight. This oversized component, roughly 10 feet in diameter, is crafted from a patchwork of blackened steel and purple-painted wood, with jagged edges that suggest it was hastily repaired multiple times. The propeller’s hub is embossed with a bold, yellow “Γ” (the gamma symbol from Waluigi’s hat), slightly dented from the airship’s final crash.

The Warped Gamma Propeller was mounted on the airship’s stern, driving it through the skies with a wobbly, unpredictable motion that matched Waluigi’s chaotic piloting style. Its blades are uneven, with one noticeably bent at a 30-degree angle, causing the airship to lurch and spin during flight—perfect for disorienting enemies but disastrous for stability. Scorch marks and embedded Bullet Bill fragments hint at its exposure to the airship’s own misfired weaponry, likely a result of Waluigi’s penchant for “tricky” battle tactics gone wrong.

When the airship went down (possibly due to a failed scheme involving Wario and a stolen Power Star), the propeller was flung free, landing in a crumpled heap amidst the wreckage. Despite its damage, it still hums faintly with residual energy, suggesting it was powered by some dubious, possibly Toad-engineered tech. The propeller’s surface is scratched with taunting graffiti, like “Waluigi #1!” and “Luigi Stinks!”, reflecting Waluigi’s spiteful rivalry. If salvaged, it could theoretically be repurposed, but its warped shape makes it more a trophy of Waluigi’s failed ambitions than a functional component.

Subtype: Trinket

Description (Player Facing): A Strange Gold Egg
Nestled within the jagged remains of a cracked-open golden dragon egg lies an unusual trinket: a shimmering gold coin, its surface etched with faint, scale-like patterns that mirror the egg’s exterior. The egg itself is a marvel, its golden shell fractured to reveal a molten glow within, as if it once held a fiery essence. The coin, however, feels oddly heavy for its size, and a subtle, almost imperceptible ticking hums from its core—a bomb cunningly disguised as treasure.

Features (GM Facing):
At the end of a long or short rest, the holder of this coin magically loses one gold coin from their inventory, as the trinket siphons wealth to fuel its hidden mechanism. A Passive Perception of 18 is required to notice that this coin differs from others—its weight is slightly off, and the scale-like etchings occasionally pulse with a faint, fiery light. If the bomb is triggered (whether by tampering, a failed investigation check, or a specific in-game condition like extreme heat), it detonates, dealing 3d6 fire damage in a 10-foot radius (Dexterity DC 15 save for half). The coin is destroyed in the explosion, leaving behind charred fragments of the golden egg shell.

You move like the wind, striking faster than your foes can see. You gain the following benefits:

  • Increase your Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution by 1, to a maximum of 20.
  • Ability Score Increase. Increase your Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution score by 1, to a maximum of 20.
  • Battlefield Dancer. Each time you hit a creature, your movement speed increases by 5 feet until the end of your turn. If you attack and hit a creature with a melee weapon attack, you can pass through its space, treating it as difficult terrain.
  • Gain the Slashing Dash special attack (below)

Slashing Dash. Active Ability (Attack)

When you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn, you can replace one of your attacks with a rapid burst of movement, moving up to 30 feet along any surface in a straight line.

You can move on vertical or horizontal surfaces with this movement, can pass through creatures, and do not provoke attacks of opportunity, but cannot pass through objects or terrain. If you are carrying a weapon you are proficient with when you take this action, each time you pass through a creature, it must make a Dexterity saving throw. A creature takes [[/damage 2d6]] + your Strength or Dexterity modifier (your choice) damage of your weapon type on a failed save, or half as much on a successful save. The number of d6 increases by one when your proficiency bonus increases (with the total number of d6 equaling your proficiency bonus).

Once you use this feature, you cannot use it again until you complete a short or long rest.

When you drink this potion, you gain the "enlarge" effect of the @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplEnlargeRed]{Enlarge/Reduce} spell for 10 minutes (no Concentration required).

The red in the potion's liquid continuously expands from a tiny bead to color the clear liquid around it and then contracts. Shaking the bottle fails to interrupt this process.

Enlarge. The target's size increases by one category—from Medium to Large, for example. The target also has Advantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. The target's attacks with its enlarged weapons or Unarmed Strikes deal an extra 1d4 damage on a hit.

Reduce. The target's size decreases by one category—from Medium to Small, for example. The target also has Disadvantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. Bonus Proficiency XGE p31[–]

When you choose this archetype at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in one of the following skills of your choice: History, Insight, Performance, or Persuasion. Alternatively, you learn one language of your choice.

Fighting Spirit XGE p31[–]

Starting at 3rd level, your intensity in battle can shield you and help you strike true. As a bonus action on your turn, you can give yourself advantage on weapon attack rolls until the end of the current turn. When you do so, you also gain 5 temporary hit points. The number of temporary hit points increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 10 at 10th level and 15 at 15th level.

You can use this feature three times, and you regain all expended uses of it when you finish a long rest.

Samurai

The Samurai is a fighter who draws on an implacable fighting spirit to overcome enemies. A Samurai's resolve is nearly unbreakable, and the enemies in a Samurai's path have two choices: yield or die fighting.

Bonus Proficiency

When you choose this archetype at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in one of the following skills of your choice: &Reference[skill=History], &Reference[skill=Insight], &Reference[skill=Performance], or &Reference[skill=Persuasion]. Alternatively, you learn one language of your choice.

Fighting Spirit

Starting at 3rd level, your intensity in battle can shield you and help you strike true. As a bonus action on your turn, you can give yourself advantage on weapon attack rolls until the end of the current turn. When you do so, you also gain 5 temporary hit points. The number of temporary hit points increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 10 at 10th level and 15 at 15th level.

You can use this feature three times, and you regain all expended uses of it when you finish a long rest.

Elegant Courtier

Starting at 7th level, your discipline and attention to detail allow you to excel in social situations. Whenever you make a Charisma (&Reference[skill=Persuasion]) check, you gain a bonus to the check equal to your Wisdom modifier.

Your self-control also causes you to gain proficiency in Wisdom saving throws. If you already have this proficiency, you instead gain proficiency in Intelligence or Charisma saving throws (your choice).

Tireless Spirit

Starting at 10th level, when you roll initiative and have no uses of Fighting Spirit remaining, you regain one use.

Rapid Strike

Starting at 15th level, you learn to trade accuracy for swift strikes. If you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn and have advantage on an attack roll against one of the targets, you can forgo the advantage for that roll to make an additional weapon attack against that target, as part of the same action. You can do so no more than once per turn.

Strength before Death

Starting at 18th level, your fighting spirit can delay the grasp of death. If you take damage that reduces you to 0 hit points and doesn't kill you outright, you can use your reaction to delay falling &Reference[condition=unconscious], and you can immediately take an extra turn, interrupting the current turn. While you have 0 hit points during that extra turn, taking damage causes death saving throw failures as normal, and three death saving throw failures can still kill you. When the extra turn ends, you fall &Reference[condition=unconscious] if you still have 0 hit points.

Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a long rest.

When you roll damage for an attack you make with a Melee weapon that you are holding with two hands, you can treat any 1 or 2 on a damage die as a 3. The weapon must have the Two-Handed or Versatile property to gain this benefit.

Variant: Spell Points

Source: Dungeon Masters Guide

With this variant system, a character who has the Spellcasting feature uses spell points instead spell slots to fuel spells. Spell points give a caster more flexibility, at the cost of greater complexity.

In this variant, each spell has a point cost based on its level. The Spell Point Cost table summarizes the cost in spell points of slots from 1st to 9th level. Cantrips don't require slots and therefore don't require spell points.

Instead of gaining a number of spell slots to cast your spells from the Spellcasting feature, you gain a pool of spell points instead. You expend a number of spell points to create a spell slot of a given level, and then use that slot to cast a spell. You can't reduce your spell points total to less than 0, and you regain all spent spell points when you finish a long rest.

Spells of 6th level and higher are particularly taxing to cast. You can use spell points to create one slot of each level of 6th or higher. You can't create another slot of the same level until you finish a long rest.

The number of spell points you have to spend is based on your level as a spellcaster, as shown in the Spell Points by Level table. Your level also determines the maximum-level spell slot you can create. Even though you might have enough points to create a slot above this maximum, you can't do so.

The Spell Points by Level table applies to bards, clerics, druids, sorcerers, and wizards. For a paladin or ranger, halve the character's level in that class and then consult the table. For a fighter (Eldritch Knight) or rogue (Arcane Trickster), divide the character's level in that class by three. 

For an Artificer, add half your levels (rounded up) in the artificer class to to determine your available spell points. (homebrew)

description.value:
1st Level &Reference[Spell Scroll]

You set an alarm against intrusion. Choose a door, a window, or an area within range that is no larger than a 20-foot Cube. Until the spell ends, an alarm alerts you whenever a creature touches or enters the warded area. When you cast the spell, you can designate creatures that won't set off the alarm. You also choose whether the alarm is audible or mental:

Audible Alarm. The alarm produces the sound of a handbell for 10 seconds within 60 feet of the warded area.

Mental Alarm. You are alerted by a mental ping if you are within 1 mile of the warded area. This ping awakens you if you're asleep.

This sturdy tankard contains a funky and earthy ale that has a savory quality to it. Like drinking a delicious broth. While it is a bit like a dark ale mixed with dried mushrooms, it's got a nice punch, and would make a filling stand-in for a meal.

Effect: Drinking just one full mug of this strange brew counts as having eaten a full package of rations. However, it also inflicts an effect from the @UUID[RollTable.f0q96i9Hwm61GDf0] table which lasts for one hour.

These arrows appear to be plants plucked from the earth, their fletching is actually delicate petals, their shafts are woody stalks, and instead of arrowheads they have knots of gnarled roots. These arrows deal bludgeoning damage instead of piercing.

If the arrow strikes a flat surface a 10ft circular patch of soft, noise muffling moss quickly grows around the impact point. Walking on this moss makes no sound, and gives advantage of stealth checks made to move quietly in that area.

Other Projectiles: These can be acquired as crossbow bolts, and the root heads can be removed to function as sling bullets, if desired.

A small, odd mushroom plucked from the grounds around the faerie manor. There's no telling how it'll taste or what it'll do if ingested.

When consumed either raw or as an ingredient in something it has a random effect from the @UUID[RollTable.f0q96i9Hwm61GDf0] table. The effect lasts for 1d4 hours.

If removed from the faerie plane these mushrooms immediately turn into mundane mushrooms with no special effects.

items.name: Spell Scroll: Scroll of Much Room

description.value:
1st Level &Reference[Spell Scroll]

This scrolls contains the arcane construction necessary to cast a modified @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells.NXWWWgHtWb7Nv21F] spell.

The scroll requires a fresh mushroom as a component, which is consumed along with the scroll at the time of casting.

The spell on the scroll causes the mushroom to grow until it creates a 10 foot radius room with fungal furniture to rest on. The structure is immobile but has a small door, and is no more resilient than a structure made of wood.

It is otherwise identical to the tiny hut spell.

Its cloudy green fluid smells of the sea and has a jellyfish-like bubble floating in it.

You can breathe underwater for 1 hour after drinking this potion.

The Samurai is a fighter who draws on an implacable fighting spirit to overcome enemies. A Samurai's resolve is nearly unbreakable, and the enemies in a Samurai's path have two choices: yield or die fighting.

@UUID[Actor.RHBq3HC3wnAxCDVu.Item.QlE1pfSqbtML9PfC]{Bonus Proficiency}

@UUID[Actor.RHBq3HC3wnAxCDVu.Item.objibRyWK0h2f73m]{Fighting Spirit}

When you choose this archetype at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in one of the following skills of your choice: &Reference[skill=History], &Reference[skill=Insight], &Reference[skill=Performance], or &Reference[skill=Persuasion]. Alternatively, you learn one language of your choice.

Starting at 3rd level, your intensity in battle can shield you and help you strike true. As a bonus action on your turn, you can give yourself advantage on weapon attack rolls until the end of the current turn. When you do so, you also gain 5 temporary hit points. The number of temporary hit points increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 10 at 10th level and 15 at 15th level.

You can use this feature three times, and you regain all expended uses of it when you finish a long rest.
For 1 hour, a candle sheds bright light in a 5-foot radius and dim light for an additional 5 feet.

As an action, you can splash the contents of this vial onto a creature within 5 feet of you or throw the vial up to 20 feet, shattering it on impact. In either case, make a ranged attack against a creature or object, treating the acid as an improvised weapon. On a hit, the target takes 2d6 acid damage.
A creature that drinks this vial of liquid gains advantage on saving throws against poison for 1 hour. It confers no benefit to undead or constructs.

This small decorated shot glass contains a swig of something stronger. A powerful shot of a faerie alcohol is contained within.

Effect: Each time you drink this you gain [[/r 1d4]] temporary hit points. Drinking additional shots increases the temporary hit gain by an additional d4 for each shot of this alcohol you've already consumed that day.

These temporary hit points follow all standard temporary hit point rules, and are not cumulative.

You can safely consume a number of these shots up to your Constitution modifier. After that, each time you take another shot you gain the poisoned condition for 1 hour (even if normally immune) and must make a DC 20 Constitution saving throw to avoid taking (2) 1d4 acid damage for every shot you've consumed that day.

A singe serving of high-end fey brandy, it smells of peaches, fig, and apples.

Effect: Upon drinking this brandy a creature must make a successful DC 16 Constitution save against a magical sleep effect. On success the creature gains a level of exhaustion but remains awake, on failure they immediately fall asleep for 1d8 hours.

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

This can effect creatures usually immune to sleep or incapable of sleeping.

A huge fig-like fruit plucked from the tree growing in the foyer of the Faerie manor. It is fragrant and probably delicious.

Once eaten, you discover that you can read and speak fluent Sylvan for 1 hour.

This long, two-handed weapon is light, the staff portion made of a flexible, woody stem. It is topped with a large flower bud of densely packed petals that are sturdy enough to serve as a bludgeon.

In its default state it deals bludgeoning damage. When this weapon is exposed to daylight (natural or magical) the flower bud blooms, revealing a blade of milky gray steel which is wickedly sharp, and remains open for the rest of the day. The Morning Glory closes itself again when night falls or it spends at least an hour in darkness.

This goblet or cup holds a single serving of red, red wine. It smells sweet as strawberries and potent alcohol.

Any creature drinking this wine must make a DC 15 Constitution saving through or suffer the poisoned condition for an hour. The potent fey magic in the wine ignores immunity.

While the creature remains poisoned they also gain proficiency in performance, as well as half proficiency in any musical instrument they pick up. If they are already proficient they gain expertise instead, and if they have expertise they instead gain advantage on any related checks.

Once the wine wears off the creature gains a level of exhaustion and loses all benefits the wine provided.

Uncommon Consumable. A bottle of extraordinarily expensive wine looted from one of the vampire dinner parties at Raventree Manor during the dimensional chaos of Highsun 16-22, 1040 BF. The label identifies it as a vintage from 687 BF (268 years old), produced in vineyards that no longer exist, from grapes cultivated by vampire lords who appreciated fine wine almost as much as fine blood. The bottle itself is a work of art—hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, sealed with wax bearing the crest of House Raventree.

When you consume this wine (drinking the full bottle takes 1 minute), you gain the following benefits for 1 hour:

  • +2 bonus to Charisma (Persuasion) and Charisma (Deception) checks (the wine's sophistication rubs off on you, somehow)
  • Advantage on saving throws against poison and disease
  • You regain 3d8 + 3 hit points as the enchanted vintage courses through your system
  • You gain darkvision out to 60 feet (if you already have darkvision, its range increases by 30 feet)
  • Your blood becomes mildly toxic to vampires for the duration—any vampire that bites you takes 2d6 necrotic damage as the enchanted wine reacts violently to their digestive process

However, the wine is also strongly associated with vampire magic. For the duration of the effect, you are treated as an undead creature for purposes of spells and effects that specifically target undead (such as Turn Undead, though you're not actually compelled to flee). This is usually not a problem for Wario, who uses the wine purely for its healing and social benefits, but it has caused awkward moments when he's been suddenly affected by a paladin's Turn Undead while trying to negotiate a deal.

Wario has approximately 8 bottles of this wine stolen from Raventree Manor's wine cellars (he would have taken more but they were heavy and he was in a hurry). He treats them as both emergency healing potions and luxury items he can sell to collectors for outrageous prices. He's already sold three bottles for 500-750gp each to merchants who didn't ask questions about provenance, and he's considering raising his prices because "clearly I'm undervaluing rare vintage vampire wine."

The wine actually tastes incredible—rich, complex, with notes of ancient oak, dark fruit, and something faintly metallic that's probably the lingering essence of the vampire blood magic used in its creation. Wario doesn't particularly appreciate fine wine (he drinks it like grape juice), but he recognizes quality when it's profitable.
description.chat: You pop the cork with your teeth—you have absolutely no respect for proper wine-opening etiquette—spit it aside, and take a long swig directly from the bottle. The wine is rich, complex, centuries of careful aging creating flavors you can't quite identify but definitely appreciate on a "this tastes expensive" level. You wipe your mouth with the back of your glove, leaving a purple-red stain. "Good stuff! WAH HA HA!" You take another swig. This is too valuable to waste on savoring, better drink it all now before someone tries to take it.

unidentified.name: Ancient Vintage Wine
unidentified.description: A bottle of extremely old wine with an ornate label in archaic script identifying it as a vintage from 687 BF. The bottle itself is beautiful hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, and the wax seal bears the crest of a noble house. The whole thing is covered in dust and decorative spiderwebs. This is clearly valuable, both as a collector's item and as a consumable of significant magical potency.

Properties: Single use item

description.value: This potion is a magic item. As a Bonus Action, you can drink it or administer it to another creature within 5 feet of yourself. The creature that drinks the magical red fluid in this vial regains 2d4 + 2 Hit Points.

A large bottle of what appears to be high-end brandy found in a fungus-filled closet in the old faerie manor. The brandy within is fragrant and inviting.

This bottle holds about 6 servings of fey brandy in it.

Effect: Upon drinking this brandy a creature must make a successful DC 16 Constitution save against a magical sleep effect. On success the creature gains a level of exhaustion but remains awake, on failure they immediately fall asleep for 1d8 hours.

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

This can effect creatures usually immune to sleep or incapable of sleeping.

A dusty bottle of wine stolen from the cellars of the Feywild Manor during the 'Satyr Eviction' (Day 25). The liquid inside shifts color from green to purple.

Effect: Consuming this wine acts as a Potion of Heroism (10 Temp HP, Bless effect), but for the next hour, the drinker cannot speak without rhyming. Failing to rhyme causes 1d4 psychic damage.
description.chat: Waluigi uncorks the bottle with his teeth. 'Time for a drink, to help me think!'

unidentified.name: Moss-Covered Wine
unidentified.description: A bottle of wine covered in moss. The label is written in Sylvan and moves when you look at it peripherally. It smells like elderberries and mischief.

description.value:
This bright red apple appears entirely harmless, and to the untrained eye there is nothing amiss about it. However, those that have glimpsed it's magical nature know that it harbors a dangerous poison.

Eating this entire apple would deal (42) 12d6 poison damage to the creature that did, and provides no nutrition whatsoever.

This apple can be divided up, which causes the damage to be divided among the pieces. A single slice of apple deals 1d6 poison damage, while half an apple would deal 6d6 poison damage, and so forth.
A slim iron key they probably unlocked a cabinet, chest, or something similar.

A trio of orange crystals that gleam with faerie energy and looks like a perpetual sunset. Touching them makes the fingertips tingle when, and imparts a lightheaded sensation not unlike being inebriated while they are held.

Rare Item (Authenticity Questionable). A stained piece of parchment covered in recipe instructions, measurements, and what appear to be flour handprints. Wario claims this is the original, authentic recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake—the cake that was so delicious it became famous throughout the Mushroom Kingdom before the war, served at royal functions, and considered one of the great culinary achievements of the pre-war era.

The recipe is written in elegant script (too elegant to be Wario's handwriting), with detailed instructions for a multi-layered strawberry cake with cream filling and decorative frosting. The measurements are in pre-war Mushroom Kingdom units, and there are marginal notes like "His Majesty preferred extra strawberries" and "Princess requests heart-shaped decoration for festivals."

The parchment shows significant age—yellowed edges, small tears, stains from what might be actual cake ingredients (or might just be random kitchen spills from whoever actually wrote this). There's a royal seal watermark visible when held up to light, which Wario points to as "proof of authenticity."

If the recipe is actually followed: Make an Intelligence check (using Cook's Utensils proficiency if you have it). On a 15 or higher, you successfully create a cake that is genuinely delicious—anyone who eats a slice regains 2d4+2 hit points and gains advantage on Charisma checks for 1 hour as they're put in a wonderful mood by the exceptional taste. On a 10-14, you create a good but not spectacular cake that provides the healing but not the Charisma bonus. On a 9 or lower, something goes wrong and you waste the ingredients.

The Authenticity Question: Wario acquired this recipe during a looting expedition to the ruins of Peach's castle sometime around 1005 BF. He claims he found it in the royal kitchens, sealed in a waterproof container, preserved perfectly for exactly this purpose. Skeptics point out that:

  • The parchment's age is inconsistent—it looks old, but not 85+ years old
  • The royal seal watermark matches Peach-era documentation, but Wario could have stolen blank royal stationery and written this himself
  • Several ingredients listed didn't become available in the Mushroom Kingdom until after Peach's death, suggesting the recipe was written later
  • Wario has been caught selling "authentic royal recipes" before, most notably "Bowser's Secret Fire Flower Chili Recipe" which turned out to be copied from a common cookbook with "add more heat" scribbled in the margins

Wario refuses to address these inconsistencies, insisting the recipe is genuine and pricing it at 5,000 gold pieces for interested buyers ("It's a piece of history! Priceless! I'm practically giving it away at 5,000!"). He's also created multiple "certified copies" that he sells for 500 gold pieces each, claiming they're "authorized reproductions" (they're just transcriptions he made himself).

The truth is ambiguous: the recipe might be authentic, might be a skilled forgery, or might be a real recipe that Wario found and is now wildly exaggerating the provenance of. The cake it produces is genuinely good regardless of authenticity, which Wario considers the only fact that matters ("Does it matter WHERE the recipe came from if the cake tastes amazing? No! Stop asking questions and pay me!").
description.chat: You carefully unfold the parchment, treating it with exaggerated reverence as if it's a sacred relic. "Behold! The ORIGINAL recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake! Used at royal banquets! Tasted by kings! Queens! That plumber guy!" You point at the flour handprints with pride. "See? These are probably Peach's ACTUAL handprints! Priceless! Historical artifact! You can't put a price on history! But if you could, it would be 5,000 gold pieces! Final offer! Non-negotiable!" You're already mentally spending the money before they've even agreed to buy it.

unidentified.name: Aged Recipe Parchment
unidentified.description: A yellowed piece of parchment containing a detailed cake recipe with elegant handwriting, marginal notes, and what appear to be flour handprints. There's a watermark visible when held to light that might be a royal seal. The recipe looks old and valuable, though verifying its claimed provenance would require expert analysis. Someone is clearly trying to sell this as more than just a cake recipe.

description.value:
This wooden weapon is sprouted from a roughly fistsized seed that's still attached to its base. A large, red thorn creates the weapon's pointed tip. Dense, thorny vines coil around the top and bottom of the haft, with small, glowing splits appearing in the wood beneath them. You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon.

In addition, this weapon has 5 charges and regains all expended charges daily at dawn. When you make a ranged attack with the weapon, you can choose to expend 1 of its charges. Hit or miss, the weapon explodes into thorny shrapnel after it reaches the target. The target and each creature within 10 feet of it must make a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw. A creatures takes [[/damage 1d8 type=piercing]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. If the target was hit by the attack, it automatically fails the saving throw. Immediately after the weapon explodes, the seed reappears at your location and regrows the weapon into your hand.

Base items. This item variant can be applied to the following base items:

  • @item[Javelin|XPHB] (@item[Ironleaf Impaler Javelin|GriffonsSaddlebag2])
  • @item[Spear|XPHB] (@item[Ironleaf Impaler Spear|GriffonsSaddlebag2])
A spell component used in @spell[Detect Poison and Disease|PHB].
A wondrous soup made by the world renowned @creature[Monstrous Soupteener|TTNSP|Soupteener]. It goes for 6 copper pieces.

A key tossed to Hjumpik by Mystic Morel after warning him not to make Toad Lee the anchor.

  • May open a route out of the manor.
  • Carries Morel’s warning as much as metal function.
  • Trust value unclear; practical value high.

On the record: received from Mystic Morel.

A key from Morel is never only a key. It is an invitation to owe uncertainty rent. — W.

Waluipedia inventory morel_feyward_key, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

The fragments left after Steely slowed, warned, and exploded near Gregory’s room.

  • May contain salvageable construct memory or parts.
  • Morale value exceeds material value.
  • Proof Hjumpik chose burial over salvage.

On the record: collected for burial.

A construct becomes a person in the moment someone chooses burial over parts. — W.

Waluipedia inventory steely_rusted_fragments, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

A heavy gold ring designed to capture souls, engraved inside the band with the initials OC. Recovered from the false Lady Aurelian — the Feyward manor’s overgrowth wearing its owner’s face — who cheerfully admitted she struck the real Aurelian in the stomach mid-flight and trapped her in the ring. Currently in Hjumpik’s custody, in the same pocket as Morel’s key, which says something unkind about Hjumpik’s pocket.

  • Captures souls. One reported occupant: the actual Lady of the manor.
  • Band engraved ‘OC’ — the same initials carved into Corvinarus bedframes.
  • Chain of custody this evening: her → Waluigi → her → Waluigi → Hjumpik.
  • Warm as a wrist, which Waluigi finds rude.

Obtained: Blown off the plant lady’s finger by an indoor Bob-omb, grabbed mid-skid by Waluigi, and deposited with the Anvil for absolutely non-negotiable custody.

On the record: party custody — not for sale, appraisal, smashing, or wearing.

Do not smash it, do not sell it, do not let Wario appraise it, and under no circumstances — including formal occasions — does anyone WEAR the soul jar. — W.

Waluipedia inventory oc_soul_ring, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from feyward_chop_bros_soul_ring_and_the_guard_with_no_name. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

waluipedia.note: party custody — not for sale, appraisal, smashing, or wearing

description.value:
A signet ring found in the grass on a table in Lady Aurelian’s dark bedroom and recognised by Hjumpik on sight. It can create and destroy connections between the fractured manors: it can speed the ritual of opening the portal, or sever the link entirely. In Hjumpik’s pocket since ~19 Harvestide, 1040 BF (Feyward time).

  • Creates or destroys connections between the manors — a key that can lock and unlock doors, install new ones and take old ones off their frames.
  • Can accelerate the portal-opening ritual, or sever the connection outright.
  • The Book of Revised History, found the same hour, warns the manors must not be combined while a star shard is in play; the ring can honour that warning or ignore it.
  • Not the OC Soul Ring — that one came off the false Lady’s finger four nights later and is a different object.

Obtained: Hjumpik bumped into a table in the dark, squished something that smelled strong, reached into the grass and found the ring under it.

On the record: in Hjumpik’s pocket — merge or sever, undecided.

The ring does not have an opinion about which function is correct. The question is not what the ring can do. The question is who gets to decide what the ring does. — W.

Waluipedia inventory raventree_signet_ring, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from feyward_dark_rooms_and_balcony_planning. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

waluipedia.note: in Hjumpik’s pocket — merge or sever, undecided

description.value:
A book Hjumpik picked out of the vegetation by the couch in Aurelian’s rooms and pocketed like a receipt from a shop. It records Raventree Manor in the 980s BF as a thriving academic centre where Toads, orcs and lightning professors exchanged ideas freely, a proto-Liberated Toads movement there ‘enlightened’ by the Iron Legion and then the Mages Guild, and a warning that the manors must not be combined while a star shard is in play.

  • Raventree in the 980s BF was a school, not a horror: Toads, orcs and lightning professors in free exchange.
  • A proto-Liberated Toads movement at Raventree was ‘enlightened’ — suppressed — by the Iron Legion and then the Mages Guild, sixty years before Order 120.
  • The manors must NOT be combined while a star shard is in play; the Oracle’s plan requires exactly that.
  • Hjumpik’s level of engagement on reading it: background lore. Waluigi’s: among the most important intelligence of the Feyward campaign.

Obtained: Resting on or near the couch, partly buried in leaves, not destroyed; Hjumpik identified it, examined it, handed it to Waluigi to read, and put it in his pocket.

On the record: pocketed like a receipt; read in full by Waluigi.

My colleagues have a persistent, infuriating habit of finding historically critical documents and treating them like grocery lists. — W.

Waluipedia inventory book_of_revised_history, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from feyward_dark_rooms_and_balcony_planning. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

waluipedia.note: pocketed like a receipt; read in full by Waluigi

description.value:
A card to Woodfellow’s library in the Feyward manor, given to Hjumpik by the goblin patron Artameer Fellow during the Revel crisis (~18 Harvestide, 1040 BF). Woodfellow issues cards only to people he assesses as genuinely knowledgeable; the return policy is one week, or the borrower becomes a book.

  • Access to Woodfellow’s library and its rare fey texts.
  • One week to return a book, or the borrower becomes a book. Woodfellow is equanimous about this.
  • Issued on an assessment of knowledge — a credential with actual standards, which Waluigi notes was not extended to Waluigi.

Obtained: Given to Hjumpik in the library after he found ‘Concerning the Nature and Sustenance of Revels Eternal’; Artameer Fellow is the patron whose previous card Wario stole to check out the Feyward Book of Many Things.

On the record: received from Artameer Fellow; nothing borrowed on it yet.

The transformation-as-late-fee system is the most effective library enforcement mechanism Waluigi has encountered in any documented plane. — W.

Waluipedia inventory woodfellow_library_card, held by Hjumpik Deldkur — filed from the_feyward_revel_crisis_poison_plants_and_frozen_diplomacy, the_feyward_revel_and_the_book_of_many_things. Mechanics as the table rules them; the archive records custody.

waluipedia.note: received from Artameer Fellow; nothing borrowed on it yet

description.value:
The wolf-pelt onesie Hjumpik has worn for three Feyward sessions. The Colour Division identified him by it from a doorway — not by description, sigil or writ — and his defence that all dwarves use wolf pelt did not land.

  • Signature garment: ‘Hey — you ARE Hjumpik. You have the signature wolf-pelt onesie on.’
  • Warm, which matters in a manor that keeps rearranging its weather.
  • Evidence, as of 2 Aethel, 922 BF (Feyward clock). Waluigi had never once thought of it as evidence.
